works.abstract: Biosolids from municipal wastewater treatment contain many contaminants of emerging concern, including microplastics (MPs), per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), pharmaceuticals and chemicals from personal care products (PPCPs). Many of these contaminants have very slow biotic or abiotic degradation rates and have been shown to have human and ecological health impacts. Application of biosolids to agriculture, a common disposal method, can result in extended environmental contamination. An approach for eliminating the contaminants is pyrolysis, which can also generate biochar, enhancing carbon sequestration as a side-benefit. We pyrolyzed biosolid samples from an operating facility at various temperatures from 400 to 700 °C with a 2-hour residence time. We then evaluated contaminant removal, which in many cases was 100 %, with only a few residuals. No trace of PFAS was detectable even at 400 °C. Overall mass removal of PPCPs, including PFAS, was over 99.9 %. MP removal via pyrolysis ranged from 91 to 97 %. The biochar contains significant amounts of Fe and P, which make it a useful fertilizer amendment. The techno-economic analysis indicates that pyrolysis may generate significant cost savings, and revenue from the sale of biochar, sufficient to more than cover the investment and operating costs of the dryer and pyrolysis unit.
works.journal: The Science of The Total Environment
works.title: Elimination of microplastics, PFAS, and PPCPs from biosolids via pyrolysis to produce biochar: Feasibility and techno-economic analysis

works.abstract: Code repository to accompany Geyer et al. (2027). Policy is essential to curb plastic pollution: the example of California's Senate Bill 54. Resources, Conservation & Recycling, 238, 109248. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.resconrec.2026.109248
works.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
works.title: Plastic consumption, waste generation, and waste management in California 1950-2050

works.abstract: As plastic pollution continues to rise, policies to curb plastic consumption and waste generation are urgently needed. Using material flow analysis, economic input-output models, and trend projection, we construct a business-as-usual baseline of plastic consumption, and plastic waste generation and management in California for 1950–2050. We then simulate the impact of source reduction, recycled content, and recycling rate mandates on plastic production, waste generation, and associated greenhouse gas emissions using California’s Senate Bill 54 as a case study. We find that, if implemented successfully, Senate Bill 54 could reduce plastic waste by nearly 56 Mt and decrease associated greenhouse gas emissions by 164 Mt CO 2 equivalent between 2025 and 2050. Our results highlight the importance of integrated, multi-faceted policy by showing the effect of policy interventions in isolation and in combination. Our modeling approach provides a broadly applicable framework to support the design and evaluation of evidence-based plastic management strategies.
works.title: Policy is essential to curb plastic pollution: the example of California’s senate Bill 54
